sections.h2: Who bills you and who sets the value
sections.html:
Two parish offices split the work. The East Baton Rouge Parish Assessor puts a value on your house. The Parish Sheriff, who doubles as tax collector, sends the notice and receives the money. The Sheriff has no say in the amount: your bill is the assessed value times the millage rates attached to your property, and voters in the parish approve the millages.

Baton Rouge is a consolidated city-parish, so one tax notice can carry parish levies, city levies and several district charges. Every city in the parish except Central collects its city taxes on the same notice, which includes Baton Rouge, Baker and Zachary.

  • Assessor (values the property): City Hall, Room 126, phone (225) 389-3920.
  • Sheriff, Tax Department (bills and collects): City Hall, 2nd Floor, 222 Saint Louis Street, Room 238; (225) 389-4810.
  • Walk-in counter at the Sheriff's tax office is staffed weekdays from 8:30 AM until 4:30 PM.

The Assessor's office does not accept payment. Send it to the Sheriff.

The state capital lies roughly 79 miles from New Orleans, along the Mississippi's eastern shore. The 2020 census counted 227,470 people in the city, the second-largest in the state, and 870,569 in the Greater Baton Rouge metro. Louisiana State University and Southern University are both based here, and state government and the river port keep housing demand steady.

Settlers built on the Istrouma Bluff, the earliest natural high ground north of the delta, to stay clear of seasonal river flooding. Flood risk is still a question buyers ask.

sections.h2: How a Baton Rouge home is assessed
sections.html:
The assessor estimates market value, studies sales of similar homes nearby, and assesses a residential property at 10% of that value. Commercial buildings are assessed at 15% of market value, which is why a rental-heavy block can show a different tax pattern from an owner-occupied one.

Millage also varies by location within the parish. Property inside city limits usually shares one rate, apart from the downtown development district, the levee district and the Comite River Diversion Canal district. Property outside the city can carry extra millages for fire protection, road lighting, garbage and the canal. Your own notice shows exactly which rates apply to your parcel.

sections.h2: Homestead exemption in East Baton Rouge Parish
sections.html:
For the house you own and live in, the first $75,000 of market value, or $7,500 assessed, is free of parish tax. City taxes and fire and crime district fees are not reduced.

The exemption is worth roughly $750 to $800 a year, depending on assessed value and the millage in your area. To qualify, you need to own the home and live in it by December 31 of the tax year. Renewal is automatic until the title changes.

Extra relief exists for some owners:

  • An owner with a service-connected disability rating of 50% through 69% gets an additional $2,500 of assessed value exempt, and 70% through 99% gets $4,500. A 100% rating exempts the full assessed value from parish tax, though city taxes and fees stay on the bill.
  • A special assessment level holds the assessed value steady for owners 65 or older who live in the house, have the homestead exemption, and report adjusted gross income of no more than $102,700.

Each tax year opens January 1 and closes with the December 31 payment deadline.

Yearly dates for East Baton Rouge Parish owners
DateWhat happens
January 1Property is assessed for condition and ownership as of this date
April 1Businesses must turn in self-reporting forms for personal property
August 15 to September 15The roll can be inspected by the public for 15 days; the Advocate prints the exact dates
November 15Louisiana Tax Commission certifies the roll; the Sheriff mails notices shortly after, usually the last week of November
December 31Taxes due; delinquent after this date, with interest at 1% per month

A postmark proves timely mailing only if the U.S. Postal Service actually canceled the envelope.

sections.h2: How to challenge a Baton Rouge assessment
sections.html:
Review the value while the books are open, then take the dispute to the Metro Council sitting as the board of review. During the 15-calendar-day inspection window the assessor's staff can discuss discrepancies in value. A call to the Assessor after August 1 will get you that year's open dates.

Whichever way the Metro Council rules, the owner or the assessor can take the case to the Louisiana Tax Commission. Board of review dates shift annually, so phone the Assessor for this year's.

sections.h2: Property tax at a Baton Rouge closing
sections.html:
Taxes get settled, not paid, when a Baton Rouge house closes. The collector never splits a bill between buyer and seller, so any arrangement between them is private. Whatever is unpaid, plus interest and fees, remains attached to the property.

State law bills the person who held the property on January 1. A buyer who closes later may find the notice still addressed to the previous owner, and it is the buyer's job to check what is owed. The Sheriff can issue a tax certificate showing taxes are paid, and an abstract of title with title insurance is advised.

  • Before signing a contract, get the balance from the Sheriff's Tax Office, (225) 389-4810.
  • When a lender escrows your taxes, request proof that it paid. Duplicate payments are not reversed, because the first one received is the one posted.
  • After the title changes, the new owner signs a new homestead application along with the closing papers.

Delinquency rules recently changed. Beginning January 1, 2026, Louisiana tax collectors auction a tax lien certificate each year instead of the property itself. Treat any delinquent balance as urgent, and ask the Sheriff how the process works now.

You can sell a house that has tax due, provided the balance is paid out of the proceeds when the title company closes. Know your numbers before you list or take an offer and nothing catches you off guard at the table.

Falling behind usually has an ordinary cause: a homestead exemption that lapsed after an inheritance, a mailing address nobody updated so notices went to a relative, or an escrow account that was never funded. If you are behind, phone the Sheriff first. After that, a title company or attorney can walk you through the payoff.

With a cash sale there is no lender underwriting, so an unpaid balance simply becomes another line on the settlement statement. Get the figure from the Sheriff's Tax Office, pass it to whoever is closing, and afterward confirm the new owner's name is on the tax roll.

faqs.q: Who do I pay property tax to in Baton Rouge?
faqs.a: You pay the East Baton Rouge Parish Sheriff, who is the tax collector. You can pay online through the link on the Sheriff's site, mail the payment with the stub, or pay in person at City Hall, 2nd Floor, 222 Saint Louis Street, Room 238, from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM on weekdays. The Assessor's Office does not accept payment.

faqs.q: When are Baton Rouge property taxes due?
faqs.a: Taxes are due by December 31 each year and are delinquent after that date, with interest at 1% per month. The Sheriff usually mails notices during the last week of November.

faqs.q: Does the Baton Rouge homestead exemption lower my city tax?
faqs.a: No. The exemption removes parish tax on the first $75,000 of market value ($7,500 assessed), but it does not apply to city taxes or to fire and crime district fees.

faqs.q: Do buyer and seller split the tax bill at a Baton Rouge closing?
faqs.a: The tax collector does not prorate between buyer and seller. Any sharing of the bill is a private arrangement handled at closing, and the full bill remains owed to the Sheriff until paid.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Baton Rouge assessment?
faqs.a: Review the assessment during the open-roll period, which runs 15 calendar days between August 15 and September 15, then bring the complaint to the Metro Council sitting as the board of review. Either side can then appeal to the Louisiana Tax Commission.
